topic.name: EGFR-mutant lung cancer: resistance to osimertinib
topic.question: New evidence on how EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer becomes resistant to osimertinib, how often each mechanism occurs, and what works after resistance.
topic.primary_query: (EGFR[tiab] OR "ErbB Receptors"[mh]) AND (osimertinib[tiab] OR AZD9291[tiab] OR Tagrisso[tiab]) AND resistan*[tiab]
topic.secondary_query: ("Drug Resistance, Neoplasm"[mh] OR "acquired resistance"[tiab] OR "disease progression"[tiab] OR progressed[tiab]) AND ("third-generation"[tiab] OR "third generation"[tiab] OR T790M[tiab] OR C797S[tiab] OR "EGFR-TKI"[tiab] OR "EGFR TKI"[tiab]) AND (NSCLC[tiab] OR "lung cancer"[tiab] OR "lung adenocarcinoma"[tiab])

criteria.text: Concerns EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer: patients, tumour samples, cell lines or animal models.
Involves osimertinib (also called AZD9291 or Tagrisso), alone or in combination.
Reports on resistance to osimertinib: a mechanism, how often a mechanism occurs, or treatment after resistance.
Reports original data (trial, cohort, case report, laboratory study) rather than being only a review, editorial or guideline.

fields.text: The resistance mechanism the paper describes, genetic or not, in the paper's words, e.g. MET amplification, ERK/GATAD2A/SAA1 axis, histological transformation.
Specific genetic alteration(s) reported, as written in the paper, e.g. EGFR C797S, MET amplification. Null if the mechanism is not a genetic alteration.
Context of the alteration, e.g. in cis or in trans with T790M, co-occurring alterations.
Treatment line or setting, e.g. first-line osimertinib, after progression.
Study design, e.g. retrospective cohort, phase 2 trial, case report, cell-line study.
Number of patients, if stated. Digits only.
What kind of finding the paper reports. Exactly one of the allowed values.
The main result in one sentence, staying as close to the paper's wording as possible.

high_impact.why: A result on what to give after resistance can change treatment, so a person always reads it. Mechanism papers are checked like any other and reach a person when a check fails.

paper.title: [Drug sensitivity analysis of monotherapy and combination therapy with Chinese and Western drugs in lung cancer organoid models].
paper.abstract: Objective: To construct patient-derived lung cancer organoid models and evaluate the sensitivity of the organoids to antitumor monotherapies, active components of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) and combined regimens of Chinese and Western drugs. Methods: A total of 10 pathologically confirmed lung adenocarcinoma specimens were collected from Tianjin Fifth Central Hospital between June 2024 and June 2025, including six surgical tumor tissue specimens and four pleural effusion samples. These samples were cultured in vitro to establish lung cancer organoid models. Morphological examination, hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining, and immunohistochemical staining were used to verify the consistence between the organoids and their parental tissues. One organoid model with available genomic profiling data (n=1) was subjected to drug sensitivity testing against commonly used antitumor drugs/regimens, and the results were compared with the clinical response. In successfully established organoid models, antitumor monotherapies (5-fluorouracil [5-FU], cisplatin and osimertinib), active components of Chinese drugs (elemene and ginsenoside Rg3) and combined regimens of Chinese and Western drugs (cisplatin plus ginsenoside Rg3 and 5-FU plus ginsenoside Rg3) were applied. Cell viability was assessed, and the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) and normalized area under the curve (AUC) values were calculated for each treatment to evaluate drug sensitivity. Results: Among the 10 samples, organoids were successfully cultured from 7 samples, and the organoids closely resembled their parental tissues in morphology and molecular marker expression. In one organoid model with increased epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene copy number gain and the EGFR p.E746_A750del mutation, sensitivity testing of commonly used antitumor drugs/regimens, including osimertinib, paclitaxel, cisplatin, the GP regimen (gemcitabine plus cisplatin), and the PP regimen (pemetrexed plus cisplatin), showed that osimertinib exhibited potent antitumor activity (IC50=1.91 μmol/L), markedly superior to the other tested drugs, and the results were consistent with the clinical response. After cryopreservation and rivival, the 7 organoid lines were continued cultured and passaged; 3 were successfully recovered. Drug sensitivity analysis of the 3 successfully established lung cancer organoid models revealed that organoids from different sources responded differently to the same drug. Osimertinib and 5-FU showed higher activity in sample 1 and sample 2, respectively, whereas sample 3 was highly resistant to cisplatin. Active components of Chinese drugs used alone showed no significant inhibitory effect, with normalized AUC values all >0.925. Combination treatment showed stronger inhibition effect in all organoid models, and IC50 values decreased to varying degrees compared with monotherapy. In samples 1 and 3, the IC50 values of cisplatin monotherapy were 152.70 and 475.00 μmol/L, respectively, and decreased to 127.30 and 121.50 μmol/L after combination treatment. Among all models, 5-FU had the lowest monotherapy IC50 among the antitumor drugs (28.08 μmol/L), which was further reduced to 11.26 μmol/L after combination treatment. Conclusion: Patient-derived lung cancer organoid models capture interindividual differences in drug sensitivity and provide a feasible approach for rapid in vitro screening of sensitive regimens and for personalized therapeutic strategies, such as combined therapy with Chinese and Western drugs.

paper.title: ERK/GATAD2A/SAA1 axis drives osimertinib resistance via NF-κB and macrophage reprogramming in EGFR-mutated lung adenocarcinoma.
paper.abstract: Background: Acquired resistance significantly limits the long-term clinical benefit of osimertinib in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). However, the early non-genetic adaptations and microenvironmental crosstalk that enable initial tumor survival remain poorly defined. This study aimed to elucidate the epigenetic-immune mechanisms driving osimertinib resistance and to identify novel actionable therapeutic targets. Methods: We integrated transcriptomic profiling and clinical cohort analyses to identify therapy-induced secreted factors during the evolution of EGFR-TKI resistance. The upstream regulatory mechanisms were characterized using ChIP, Co-IP, and dual-luciferase reporter assays. The dual functional roles of the identified factor, serum amyloid A1 (SAA1), in tumor-intrinsic signaling and macrophage polarization were investigated in vitro. Finally, the therapeutic efficacy of combining SAA1 neutralization with osimertinib was evaluated across patient-derived organoids, xenografts, and immunocompetent spontaneous lung tumor models. Results: We identified SAA1 as a critical therapy-induced secreted factor that progressively increases during the transition from drug tolerance to established resistance, which negatively correlates with clinical outcomes in patients receiving osimertinib. Mechanistically, osimertinib treatment suppressed the ERK-dependent phosphorylation of the transcriptional repressor GATAD2A at Ser114. This event destabilized the NuRD complex, thereby relieving the epigenetic transcriptional repression of SAA1. Secreted SAA1 promoted therapeutic resistance through dual mechanisms: activating the autocrine TLR4/NF-κB survival signaling in tumor cells and inducing the paracrine polarization of pro-tumorigenic SPP1+ macrophages. Therapeutically, targeted neutralization of SAA1 synergized robustly with osimertinib to reverse immunosuppressive remodeling and induce profound tumor regression in multiple preclinical models. Conclusions: Our findings define a novel therapy-induced ERK/GATAD2A/SAA1 epigenetic-immune axis that drives acquired resistance to osimertinib. SAA1 acts as a pivotal bridge between tumor-intrinsic survival adaptations and microenvironmental immune suppression, highlighting SAA1 neutralization as a tractable combinatorial strategy to enhance EGFR-TKI efficacy in LUAD.

paper.title: Osimertinib Plus Platinum-based Chemotherapy in Patients With EGFR-Mutated Advanced NSCLC Post-progression on First-Line Osimertinib: ORCHARD.
paper.abstract: Background: ORCHARD (NCT03944772) was a biomarker-directed, phase II, platform study conducted to characterize resistance mechanisms and evaluate novel treatment combinations in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) following progression on first-line osimertinib. We report results from the module evaluating osimertinib plus platinum-based chemotherapy. Methods: Patients received osimertinib (80 mg once daily) plus ≤ 4 cycles of platinum-based doublet chemotherapy (pemetrexed 500 mg/m2 plus carboplatin AUC5) on day 1 of every 21-day cycle, followed by pemetrexed maintenance until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or another discontinuation criterion. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1. Secondary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS), duration of response (DoR), overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Thirty-one patients received study treatment. Eight patients had a confirmed partial response (ORR 26%; 80% CI, 16-39). Median DoR was 7.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-not calculable). Median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 4.0-7.5); PFS events were reported in 29 (94%) patients. Median OS was 10.9 months (95% CI, 8.5-15.0); 20 (65%) patients had died at data cut-off. Grade ≥ 3 adverse events (AEs) occurred in 20 (65%) patients; AEs leading to discontinuation of any treatment occurred in 7 (23%) patients. Conclusion: In patients with EGFR-mutated advanced NSCLC who had progressed on first-line osimertinib, osimertinib plus platinum-based chemotherapy demonstrated a modest clinical benefit and manageable safety profile, consistent with the individual drug profiles.

paper.title: Development of Potent and Selective EGFR-PROTACs Based on Macrocyclic Fourth-Generation EGFR Inhibitors.
paper.abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutant-driven non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) frequently develops acquired resistance to third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), particularly through the EGFR C797S mutation. Existing EGFR-targeting proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) remain limited by unfavorable pharmacokinetics and suboptimal selectivity inherited from their parent TKIs. To address these limitations, we developed HQY1480, a next-generation PROTAC derived from the macrocyclic fourth-generation EGFR inhibitor BI-4020. Systematic linker and E3 ligase ligand optimization enabled potent and selective degradation of multiple clinically relevant EGFR mutants with single-digit nanomolar DC50 values. HQY1480 exhibited favorable pharmacokinetics, stronger suppression of oncogenic signaling than BI-4020, and no detectable off-target degradation in proteomic profiling. In xenograft models, HQY1480 outperformed BI-4020, overcame osimertinib resistance, and effectively inhibited tumor growth at low doses, while inducing robust EGFR degradation in patient-derived xenografts. These findings establish HQY1480 as an effective and well-tolerated lead PROTAC for EGFR-mutant NSCLC with acquired resistance to third-generation TKIs.

paper.title: Antibody-drug conjugates after EGFR-TKI resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC: Evidence boundaries, post-progression reassessment, and therapeutic sequencing.
paper.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are emerging therapeutic options for epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) after the development of resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). However, the founding EGFR alteration alone does not guide ADC selection. At progression, actionable resistance mechanisms, altered antigen expression, central nervous system (CNS) involvement, spatial heterogeneity, and histological transformation may shift treatment priorities. This narrative review links agent-specific evidence boundaries to an eight-domain assessment of the post-progression disease state and distinguishes ADC eligibility from therapeutic priority. The framework first identifies clinical scenarios requiring immediate local, CNS-directed, or lineage-specific treatment. It then evaluates resistance-directed therapy and other systemic options in the context of prior treatment. Finally, each ADC is assessed according to its evidence base, biomarkers, construct fit, disease distribution, availability, and patient-specific safety. Currently, selected TROP2-directed ADCs have the most mature evidence. HER3-directed therapy remains under investigation, whereas c-Met- and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-directed ADCs may be relevant in biomarker-defined settings. Tissue biopsy, plasma circulating tumor DNA analysis, and selected cerebrospinal fluid testing should be considered when the findings could alter clinical management. Accordingly, ADCs should be positioned relative to competing local and systemic strategies rather than considered a uniform post-osimertinib class. Prospective validation is required to determine whether this framework improves treatment outcomes.

paper.title: MMP14-mediated proteolytic cleavage of LAMC2 domain III fragment drives osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer.
paper.abstract: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a critical clinical challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with 40%-60% of progressing patients lacking an identifiable genetic resistance driver. Through quantitative secretomic profiling of paired osimertinib-sensitive and -resistant NSCLC cell lines, we identified laminin subunit γ2 (LAMC2) as markedly enriched in resistant cell secretomes. Single-cell RNA sequencing reanalysis revealed a LAMC2-high drug-tolerant persister subpopulation that expanded under osimertinib pressure, with pseudotime analysis suggesting progressive co-upregulation of LAMC2 and matrix metalloproteinase 14 (MMP14) along the treatment-to-resistance trajectory. Across four independent cohorts, MMP14 exhibited the strongest co-expression with LAMC2 among all metalloproteinases; the two proteins also physically interacted, and their concurrent high expression predicted the worst overall survival. Mechanistically, MMP14 cleaved LAMC2 to release a bioactive Domain III (DIII) fragment harboring EGF-like repeats, which reactivated EGFR/AKT/ERK signaling despite continued osimertinib exposure. Exogenous DIII conferred resistance in sensitive cells, whereas an anti-DIII blocking antibody reversed MMP14-driven resistance in cell lines and patient-derived organoids. The selective MMP14 inhibitor NSC405020 restored osimertinib sensitivity in vitro and suppressed xenograft growth. In residual tumor tissues from neoadjuvant osimertinib-treated patients, non-responders exhibited higher LAMC2/MMP14 co-expression and more prominent spatial exclusion of CD8+ T-cells from the tumor core compared with major pathological responders. These findings identify the MMP14-LAMC2-DIII proteolytic axis as a non-genetic resistance mechanism and suggest that MMP14 inhibition or DIII neutralization may represent a rational strategy to overcome acquired osimertinib resistance.

paper.title: Dalmelitinib Plus Aumolertinib in Advanced NSCLC Patients With EGFR-TKI Resistance and MET Amplification: A Randomized Phase 3 Trial.
paper.abstract: Purpose: MET amplification accounts for up to 30% of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKI, especially following third-generation EGFR-TKI treatment, yet precision-targeted therapeutic options remain limited. Early-phase studies demonstrated promising antitumor activity with the MET-TKI dalmelitinib combined with the third-generation EGFR-TKI aumolertinib. This phase 3 trial compared dalmelitinib-aumolertinib with platinum-based chemotherapy in EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified advanced NSCLC after EGFR-TKIs progression. Patients and methods: This randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial (NCT06110663) enrolled patients with locally advanced or metastatic EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified NSCLC after EGFR-TKI progression. MET amplification was defined by fluorescence in situ hybridization as a mean MET copy number ≥5 or MET/CEP7 ratio ≥2. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to dalmelitinib-aumolertinib or platinum-based chemotherapy groups. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review per RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included overall survival, objective response rate (ORR), duration of response (DoR), and safety. Results: A total of 314 enrolled patients were assigned to dalmelitinib-aumolertinib (n=156) or platinum-based chemotherapy (n=158). Median follow-up was 11.2 months at the data cutoff date (December 10, 2025). Median PFS was 6.2 months with dalmelitinib-aumolertinib and 4.4 months with chemotherapy (HR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.45 to 0.81; P <0.001). Corresponding ORRs were 59.6% and 38.6%, and median DoRs were 9.7 months and 4.4 months, respectively. Overall survival data were immature. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 50.0% and 51.0% of patients, respectively. Toxicity profiles differed, with more hepatic laboratory abnormalities with dalmelitinib-aumolertinib and more hematologic toxicities with chemotherapy. Conclusion: The dalmelitinib-aumolertinib combination significantly improved PFS versus chemotherapy, with a manageable safety profile in advanced EGFR-mutated, MET-amplified NSCLC after progression on EGFR-TKI. These findings support dual EGFR/ MET inhibition as a new treatment option in this biomarker selected population.

paper.title: Firmonertinib 160mg in EGFR-Mutated NSCLC with Brain Metastases After EGFR-TKI Resistance (iFORCE): Clinical Outcomes and Mechanistic Insights.
paper.abstract: Background: Brain metastases (BM) are frequent in EGFR-mutated (EGFRm) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and remain challenging after prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. This exploratory study evaluated high-dose fimmonertinib and explored subtype-specific spatial biology. Methods: iFORCE was a prospective, single-center, single-arm study. Eligible patients had advanced NSCLC harboring EGFR mutations with previously treated BM following EGFR-TKI therapy, or intracranial disease progression. Patients received 160 mg firmonertinib once daily. The primary endpoint was intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS). Archival paired primary tumors and BM specimens from an independent retrospective cohort underwent exploratory digital spatial profiling (DSP). Results: Twenty-three patients were enrolled. At a median follow-up of 19.7 months (95% CI, 14.5-25.3), median iPFS was 14.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-not estimable [NE]), with 12- and 18-month iPFS rates of 53.8% and 46.1%, respectively. Based on the best intracranial overall response, intracranial objective response and disease control rates were 34.8% (95% CI, 16.4-57.3) and 91.3% (95% CI, 72.0-98.9). Median systemic PFS was 10.7 months (95% CI, 3.9-NE). Treatment-related adverse events occurred in 13 (56.5%) patients, mostly grade 1; one patient (4.3%) developed grade 3 stomatitis. No treatment discontinuations or treatment-related deaths were observed. DSP revealed distinct EGFR subtype-specific BM ecosystems: exon 19 deletion tumors retained immune-enriched inflammatory programs, whereas L858R-mutated tumors showed tumor-intrinsic cell-cycle, DNA-repair, RNA-splicing, apoptosis-resistance, and immune-evasion features. Conclusions: Fimonertinib 160 mg showed promising intracranial activity with a manageable safety profile in EGFR-TKI-treated EGFRm NSCLC with BM. L858R BM displayed tumor-intrinsic, microenvironment-independent biology, suggesting preferential sensitivity to high-dose firmonertinib.
